meta.exam_info: ★★ HIGH WEIGHTAGE — 2 MCQs · Q2 Short Questions

blocks.head: Two Key Rules to Memorise
items: Period number = Shell number (n) — how many electron shells the atom has.
Group number = Number of valence electrons — for main-group (s and p block) elements.

blocks.head: How to Write Config from Position
blocks.body: Given: Period 3, Group 13 — Period 3 → 3 shells. Group 13 → 3 valence electrons (2 in 3s + 1 in 3p). Fill in order: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹ → this is Al (Aluminium).
items: Rule: p-block starts at Group 13. Group 13 → ns²np¹, Group 14 → ns²np², up to Group 18 → ns²np⁶ (noble gas)

blocks.t: A common SAQ: 'Identify the element in Period 4 and Group 17.' → n=4, Group 17 → 7 valence electrons, p-block. Config: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²4p⁵ → Bromine (Br). Always write full config AND name the element.

items.q: An element is in Period 3 and Group 16. Identify it and write its full electronic configuration.
items.ans: Period 3 → n=3 (3 shells). Group 16 → 6 valence electrons, p-block (6 = 2 in s + 4 in p). Config: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁴ → Sulfur (S), Z=16.

items.q: Which block does an element in Group 7 belong to? How many valence electrons?
items.ans: Group 7 is in the d-block (transition metals, Groups 3–12). A d-block element has electrons filling the (n−1)d subshell. It has 7 valence electrons when counting both 4s and 3d electrons (e.g., Mn: [Ar]3d⁵4s² → 7 valence electrons).

items.q: State the period and group of an element with configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p³.
items.ans: Outermost shell: n=3 → Period 3. Valence electrons: 3s²3p³ = 5 → Group 15. This is Phosphorus (P), Z=15.

blocks.label: Modern Periodic Law
blocks.text: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

blocks.t: 1.7.1 Atomic Radius

blocks.label: Atomic Radius
blocks.text: The atomic radius is a measure of the size of an atom. It is half of the distance between two identical atoms bonded together.

blocks.t: Unit: picometer (pm) or Angstrom (Å)

items.title: Number of Shells
items.body: — More shells → larger atom. Each new period adds a shell → radius increases going down a group.

items.title: Effective Nuclear Charge (Z<sub>eff</sub>)
items.body: — Higher Z<sub>eff</sub> pulls electron cloud inward → smaller radius. Increases across a period.

items.title: Shielding Effect
items.body: — Inner electrons shield valence electrons from nucleus. More shielding → less pull → larger radius. Increases going down a group.

cards.across_note: Nuclear charge ↑, same shell → electrons pulled closer
cards.down_note: New shell added; shielding outweighs nuclear charge increase

cards.body:
Na > Mg > Al > Si > P > S > Cl > Ar

Largest: Na · Smallest: Ar (noble gas has no covalent radius)

blocks.t: If asked 'why does atomic radius decrease across a period?' — mention: (1) nuclear charge increases, (2) same number of shells, (3) valence electrons are pulled inward.
1.7.2 Ionic Radius

blocks.label: Ionic Radius
blocks.text: The ionic radius is a measure of the size of an ion in a crystal lattice. It is defined as the distance from the nucleus of an ion to the outermost electron shell, measured in picometer (pm) or angstrom (Å).

blocks.head: Cation vs Anion Size
items: Cation (loses e⁻): Fewer electrons, same protons → nucleus pulls remaining electrons more strongly → smaller than parent atom. May lose an entire shell (e.g., Na → Na⁺ loses 3rd shell entirely).
Anion (gains e⁻): More electrons, same protons → electron-electron repulsion increases → cloud expands → larger than parent atom.
Key values: Na (186 pm) → Na⁺ (95 pm); O (66 pm) → O²⁻ (140 pm)

blocks.t: Isoelectronic series (all 10 electrons): Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Ne, F⁻, O²⁻, N³⁻. Order of size: Al³⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < Ne ≈ F⁻ < O²⁻ < N³⁻. More protons with same electrons = smaller size.
1.7.3 Ionization Energy

blocks.label: 1st Ionization Energy
blocks.text: The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of atoms of the element in the gaseous state to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions is known as 1st ionization energy (ΔH<sub>i1</sub>).

blocks.t:
Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻    ΔH_i1 = +494 kJ mol⁻¹
Ca(g) → Ca⁺(g) + e⁻    ΔH_i1 = +590 kJ mol⁻¹
Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻  ΔH_i2 = +1150 kJ mol⁻¹
Ca²⁺(g) → Ca³⁺(g) + e⁻ ΔH_i3 = +4940 kJ mol⁻¹

items.title: Nuclear Charge
items.body: — Greater effective nuclear charge → harder to remove electron → higher IE.

items.title: Atomic Size
items.body: — Larger atom → electron farther from nucleus → weaker hold → lower IE.

items.title: Electronic Arrangement
items.body: — Half-filled and fully-filled subshells are extra stable → higher IE. Noble gases have highest IE in each period.

items.title: Shielding Effect
items.body: — More inner electrons shield valence electron → weaker pull → lower IE.

items.title: Spin-Pair Repulsion
items.body: — Paired electrons in same orbital repel each other → slightly easier to remove → lower IE. This explains why O < N and S < P.

blocks.head: The N > O Anomaly — Most Common Board Question
blocks.eq:
₇N = 1s² 2s² 2p_x¹ 2p_y¹ 2p_z¹  (half-filled 2p — extra stable)  IE = 1403 kJ mol⁻¹
₈O = 1s² 2s² 2p_x² 2p_y¹ 2p_z¹  (one paired e⁻, spin-pair repulsion) IE = 1365 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.note: Oxygen's paired electron in 2px experiences repulsion from its partner → easier to remove → O has lower first IE than N despite higher atomic number.

cards.across_note: Exception: Group 2→3 (Be>B, Mg>Al) drop; Group 15→16 (N>O, P>S) drop

cards.body:
• Single valence electron
• Large atomic size
• Strong shielding by inner shells
→ Easiest to ionize

blocks.t: Be > B and Mg > Al: Be (1s²2s²) has fully-filled 2s — extra stable. B has 2s²2p¹ — the 2p electron is in a higher energy subshell AND shielded by 2s electrons → easier to remove. Same logic for Mg > Al.
1.7.4 Electron Affinity (ΔH°ea)

blocks.label: First Electron Affinity
blocks.text: The first electron affinity (ΔH°ea1) is the enthalpy change involved when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous uni-negative ions under standard conditions.

blocks.t:
Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)     ΔH°ea1 = −348.8 kJ mol⁻¹  (exothermic, energy RELEASED)
O(g) + e⁻  → O⁻(g)      ΔH°ea1 = −142 kJ mol⁻¹
O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g)     ΔH°ea2 = +844 kJ mol⁻¹   (endothermic, energy ABSORBED)

blocks.head: BOOK ERROR — Page 10
blocks.wrong: Book says: '798 kJ mol⁻¹ of energy is absorbed when second electron is added to O⁻'
blocks.correct: Correct value (also in book's own equation): ΔH°ea2 = +844 kJ mol⁻¹
blocks.reason: The value 798 is a printing error. The book's own equation on the same page shows +844 kJ mol⁻¹. Write +844 in exams.

blocks.head: Why 2nd EA is Always Positive?
blocks.body: O⁻ already carries a negative charge. Adding another electron means forcing a second negative charge onto an already-negative ion — the repulsion is enormous. Energy must be supplied (endothermic) → ΔH°ea2 is always positive for O²⁻, S²⁻, etc.

cards.across_note: Exceptions: Group 2 (full s), Group 15 (half-filled p), Group 18
cards.down_note: F vs Cl anomaly: Cl has more negative EA than F

cards.body:
F is smaller but has very compact 2p orbitals → incoming electron experiences strong repulsion in crowded 2p shell → less energy released

Cl: −349 kJ/mol · F: −328 kJ/mol
Cl has more negative EA

blocks.t: 1.7.5 Electronegativity

blocks.label: Electronegativity
blocks.text: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract shared pair of electrons toward itself in a molecule.

blocks.t: Scale: Pauling Scale (dimensionless, 0.8–4.0). Most electronegative: F (4.0). Most electropositive: Cs (0.8).

items.title: Atomic Size
items.body: — Larger atom → shared electrons farther from nucleus → weaker attraction → lower electronegativity.

items.title: Effective Nuclear Charge
items.body: — Higher Zeff → stronger pull on bonding electrons → higher electronegativity.

blocks.head: Pauling's Nobel Prizes
items: Linus Pauling won two Nobel Prizes — Chemistry (1954) for work on chemical bonding, and Peace (1962) for opposing nuclear weapons. The only person to win two unshared Nobel Prizes.

blocks.t: 1.7.6 Variation in Metallic Character
Metallic character = tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions (electropositive character).

cards.across_note: ↑ nuclear charge, ↓ size → harder to lose electrons
cards.down_note: ↑ size, ↑ shielding → easier to lose valence electrons

cards.body:
IE ↑ · EA ↑ (more −ve) · EN ↑ · Radius ↓ · Metallic character ↓

DOWN GROUP ↓:
IE ↓ · EA ↓ (less −ve) · EN ↓ · Radius ↑ · Metallic character ↑

items.q: Arrange in increasing order of atomic radius: Na, Cl, K, Ar.
items.ans:
Cl < Ar < Na < K

Across Period 3: Na > Cl > Ar (radius decreases →). Ar is smallest in Period 3 (noble gas, no covalent radius but effectively smallest). Going down Group 1: K > Na. So overall: Cl < Ar < Na < K.

items.q: Why is the IE of N (1403 kJ/mol) greater than O (1365 kJ/mol), even though O has a higher atomic number?
items.ans:
N has a half-filled 2p subshell (2p³ — one electron in each p orbital), which is extra stable. Removing an electron disrupts this stability → high IE.

O has a paired electron in one 2p orbital → this paired electron experiences spin-pair repulsion from its partner → it is slightly easier to remove → lower IE than N.

items.q: The 2nd electron affinity of oxygen (O²⁻) is positive (+844 kJ/mol). Explain why.
items.ans: O⁻ already carries a negative charge. Adding a 2nd electron means forcing another negative charge onto a negative ion. The repulsion between the incoming electron and the existing negative charge is enormous. Energy must be supplied (endothermic) → ΔH°ea2 is positive.

items.q: Why does Cl have a more negative EA than F, even though F is smaller?
items.ans:
F has very compact 2p orbitals. When an incoming electron enters F's already-crowded 2p subshell, it experiences strong electron-electron repulsion → less energy is released.

Cl has larger 3p orbitals → more space → incoming electron experiences less repulsion → more energy released → EA of Cl (−349 kJ/mol) is more negative than F (−328 kJ/mol).

blocks.t: Na is more reactive than Mg — lower IE (496 vs 738 kJ/mol), larger size, single valence electron, greater metallic character.
With Water
With Oxygen

rxns.note: only under limited O₂ or high temp

blocks.head: Why Sodium is Stored in Kerosene Oil?
blocks.body: Na reacts vigorously with air (forming Na₂O₂) and moisture. Kerosene oil is non-reactive with Na, prevents contact with air and water.

blocks.t: With Chlorine

rxns.note: white solid; less vigorous than Na

blocks.head: Why Na is More Reactive Than Mg
items: Na has 1 valence electron vs Mg's 2 → Na loses electron more easily
Na has lower IE₁ (496 kJ/mol) vs Mg (738 kJ/mol)
Na has larger atomic radius → valence electron farther from nucleus → weaker pull
Na achieves noble gas configuration (like Ne) by losing just 1 electron; Mg needs to lose 2

blocks.t: For the Q3 reactions question: write all 6 equations, then compare reactivity: Na > Mg due to (1) larger size, (2) lower IE, (3) fewer valence electrons, (4) greater metallic character. Board expects equations + reasoning.

items.q: Write the equation for the reaction of Mg with steam.
items.ans:
Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g)

Mg reacts vigorously with steam (not cold water) to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas.

items.q: What is the main product when Na burns in excess O₂? Write the equation.
items.ans:
2Na(s) + O₂(g) → 2Na₂O₂(s)

Main product is sodium peroxide (Na₂O₂) — a yellowish-white solid. The reaction burns with a golden-yellow flame. Na₂O only forms under limited O₂ or at high temperature.

items.q: Give TWO reasons why Na reacts more vigorously with Cl₂ than Mg does.
items.ans:
1. Lower IE₁: Na (494 kJ/mol) vs Mg (738 kJ/mol) → Na loses its valence electron more easily → reacts more readily with Cl₂.

2. Fewer valence electrons: Na has only 1 valence electron to lose (achieves Ne configuration immediately), while Mg must lose 2 electrons → Na's reaction is thermodynamically easier and faster.

sections.title: Trends in Bonding in Oxides and Chlorides of Period 3

blocks.t: Across Period 3, bonding shifts from ionic → covalent as the electronegativity difference between the element and oxygen/chlorine decreases.

blocks.head: Bonding Trend
items: Groups 1, 2, 3 (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃): Mostly ionic — giant ionic lattices.
Groups 4–7 (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃, SiCl₄, PCl₅): Mostly covalent — discrete covalent molecules.

blocks.t: 1.9.1 Classification of Oxides

blocks.label: Basic Oxide
blocks.text: A basic oxide is an oxide that when combined with water gives off an alkali.

blocks.label: Acidic Oxide
blocks.text: An acidic oxide is an oxide that when combined with water gives off an acid.

blocks.label: Amphoteric Oxide
blocks.text: Amphoteric oxides are oxides that can react with both acids and bases.

blocks.t: 1.9.2 Classification of Chlorides

blocks.head: Why NaCl is Neutral but AlCl₃ is Acidic?
items: NaCl: Na⁺ is large with low charge → does not polarise water → no hydrolysis → neutral (pH=7).
AlCl₃: Al³⁺ is small and highly charged (3+) → strongly polarises surrounding water molecules → releases H⁺ (hydrolysis) → acidic solution.
Rule: The more polarising the cation (small size + high charge), the more acidic its chloride solution.

blocks.t: ZnO is a common exam bonus example — it's amphoteric: reacts with both HCl (→ ZnCl₂ + H₂O) and NaOH (→ Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂O).

items.q: Classify these oxides as basic, acidic, or amphoteric: Na₂O, Al₂O₃, SO₃, ZnO.
items.ans:
Na₂O — Basic oxide (Na is a metal, Group 1). Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH.

Al₂O₃ — Amphoteric oxide. Reacts with both HCl (→ AlCl₃) and NaOH (→ NaAlO₂).

SO₃ — Acidic oxide (S is a non-metal). SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.

ZnO — Amphoteric oxide. Reacts with HCl (→ ZnCl₂) and NaOH (→ Na₂ZnO₂).

items.q: Why does AlCl₃ solution have an acidic pH while NaCl solution has pH = 7?
items.ans:
NaCl: Na⁺ is large with low charge density → does not polarise water molecules → no hydrolysis → neutral (pH=7).

AlCl₃: Al³⁺ is small and highly charged (+3) → high charge density → strongly polarises surrounding water molecules → Al³⁺ pulls electron density from O–H bonds → H⁺ ions released into solution → acidic pH.

items.q: Write the equation showing SiCl₄ reacting with water. What type of chloride is this?
items.ans:
SiCl₄(ℓ) + 2H₂O(ℓ) → SiO₂(s) + 4HCl(aq)

SiCl₄ is an acidic chloride. It is a covalent chloride (Si is a non-metal) that undergoes hydrolysis with water to produce HCl → acidic solution.

sections.title: Variation in Oxidation Number in Oxides and Chlorides

blocks.label: Oxidation Number
blocks.text: The oxidation number of an atom is the formal charge on that atom in a molecule or ion.

blocks.t: For Period 3 elements: oxidation number = group number. Oxygen (−2) and chlorine (−1) are always more electronegative → element always carries positive oxidation number.

blocks.head: Why P and S Show Variable Oxidation States?
blocks.body: P and S are in Period 3 and have empty 3d orbitals available. Electrons can be promoted into these 3d orbitals, allowing more electrons to participate in bonding (octet expansion):
items: S: Can use 2, 4, or 6 electrons → oxidation states +2, +4, +6
Na, Mg, Al have no accessible d-orbitals → fixed oxidation states only

blocks.t: Calculation: S in SO₄²⁻ → S + 4(−2) = −2 → S = +6. S in SO₂ → S + 2(−2) = 0 → S = +4. Formula: (ox. no. of element) + (no. of O × −2) = charge of species.

items.q: Calculate the oxidation number of: (i) P in H₃PO₄   (ii) S in H₂SO₄   (iii) Cl in HClO₃
items.ans:
(i) P in H₃PO₄: 3(+1) + P + 4(−2) = 0 → 3 + P − 8 = 0 → P = +5

(ii) S in H₂SO₄: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0 → 2 + S − 8 = 0 → S = +6

(iii) Cl in HClO₃: (+1) + Cl + 3(−2) = 0 → 1 + Cl − 6 = 0 → Cl = +5

items.q: Why do Na and Mg have fixed oxidation states while P and S show variable ones?
items.ans:
Na and Mg are in Period 3 but their d-orbitals are at much higher energy and not accessible for bonding → can only use fixed number of valence electrons → fixed oxidation states (+1 for Na, +2 for Mg).

P and S have empty 3d orbitals at relatively low energy. Electrons from the ground state can be promoted into these 3d orbitals → more electrons participate in bonding → variable oxidation states (P: +3, +5; S: +2, +4, +6).

items.q: What is the oxidation state of S in Na₂SO₃ and Na₂S₂O₃?

mcqs.q: Which one is correct about metallic character?
opts: Decreases top to bottom in group
Increases top to bottom in group
Remains constant left to right in period
Increases left to right in period
mcqs.exp: Going down a group, atomic size and shielding increase → easier to lose electrons → metallic character increases.

mcqs.q: Which property increases as you go down a group?
mcqs.exp: Atomic radius increases down a group as new shells are added. IE, EA, EN all decrease going down.

mcqs.q: Which conditions result in higher ionization energy?
opts: Smaller atom and greater nuclear charge
Smaller atom and smaller nuclear charge
Larger atom and greater nuclear charge
Larger atom and smaller nuclear charge
mcqs.exp: Smaller atom = electron closer to nucleus = harder to remove. Greater nuclear charge = stronger pull. Both increase IE.

mcqs.q: Which atom shows variable (more than one) oxidation states?
mcqs.exp: P has empty 3d orbitals → can expand octet → shows +3 (PCl₃) and +5 (PCl₅). Na, Mg, Al have fixed oxidation states.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct general trend in electron affinity in a group?
opts: It becomes less negative from top to bottom
It becomes more negative from top to bottom
mcqs.exp: Going down a group, atomic size increases → incoming electron attracted less strongly → EA becomes less negative (smaller magnitude).

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of sulfur in SO₄²⁻?
Which is the correct trend for electronegativity across a period?
mcqs.exp: Across a period, nuclear charge increases and atomic size decreases → greater pull on bonding electrons → higher EN.

mcqs.q: The atomic radius generally _____ across a period.
mcqs.exp: Increasing nuclear charge across a period (same shell) → electrons pulled closer → decreasing atomic radius.

mcqs.q: Which element has the highest ionization energy in Period 3?
mcqs.exp: Ar is a noble gas with completely filled shells (3s²3p⁶) → extremely stable → extremely high IE.

mcqs.q: When sodium burns in excess oxygen, the main product is:
mcqs.exp: Na burns vigorously in O₂ to form sodium peroxide (Na₂O₂). Na₂O only forms under limited O₂.

mcqs.q: Which chloride undergoes hydrolysis in water to give an acidic solution?
mcqs.exp: Al³⁺ is small and highly charged → polarises water → hydrolysis → releases H⁺ → acidic.

mcqs.q: The ionic radius of Na⁺ compared to the Na atom is:
mcqs.exp: Na loses its entire 3rd shell when forming Na⁺ → drops from 3 to 2 shells → much smaller (Na=186 pm; Na⁺=95 pm).

sqs.q: What is 1st ionization energy? Give an example.
sqs.a:
Definition: The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

Example:

Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ ΔH_i1 = +494 kJ mol⁻¹

Always positive (endothermic) — energy must be supplied to overcome nucleus–electron attraction.

sqs.q: Explain why sulfur has a lower first IE than phosphorus.
sqs.a:
Phosphorus has a half-filled 3p subshell (3s²3p³ — one electron per p orbital) — extra stable due to exchange energy and symmetry. Removing an electron from this configuration requires more energy.

Sulfur (3s²3p⁴) has a paired electron in one 3p orbital experiencing spin-pair repulsion from its partner → easier to remove.

P: [Ne] 3s² 3p¹ 3p¹ 3p¹ (half-filled — stable) IE₁ = higher S: [Ne] 3s² 3p² 3p¹ 3p¹ (one paired e⁻ — repulsion) IE₁ = lower

sqs.q: What are the factors that affect electronegativity?
sqs.a:
1. Atomic Size: Larger atom → shared electrons farther from nucleus → weaker attraction → lower EN. (E.g., Cs has lowest EN — largest atom in Group 1.)

2. Effective Nuclear Charge (Zeff): Higher Zeff → stronger pull on bonding electrons → higher EN.

F (smallest in Period 2, highest Zeff) has highest EN of all elements (4.0 Pauling).

sqs.q: What factors are responsible for the increasing reactivity of alkali metals down the group?
sqs.a:
• Increasing atomic size: Valence electron farther from nucleus → weaker hold → easier to lose.
  • Increasing shielding: More inner shells → effectively reduces nuclear pull on valence electron.
  • Decreasing IE: Less energy needed to remove valence electron → more reactive.

Result: Cs is far more reactive than Na or Li (e.g., Cs reacts explosively with water).

sqs.q: Why do some elements show variable oxidation numbers while others do not?
sqs.a:
Elements in Period 3 and beyond (P, S, Cl) have empty d-orbitals available. Electrons can be promoted into these with relatively little energy → more electrons available for bonding → variable oxidation states.

Examples: S shows +2, +4, +6; P shows +3, +5.

By contrast, Period 2 elements (Na, Mg) and Group 1/2 elements have no accessible d-orbitals → only one stable oxidation state (Na always +1, Mg always +2).

sqs.q: Why are oxides of sodium and magnesium more ionic than oxides of nitrogen and phosphorus?
sqs.a:
Ionic character depends on electronegativity difference between the element and oxygen:

  • Na (EN=0.9) and Mg (EN=1.2) have very low EN → large difference with O (3.5) → predominantly ionic bonding → ionic oxides.
  • N (EN=3.0) and P (EN=2.1) have higher EN → smaller difference with O → covalent bonding → covalent oxides.

Na and Mg are metals (left side of PT) → lose electrons readily → form ionic compounds. N and P are non-metals → share electrons.

sqs.q: Give reasons for different reactivities of Na and Mg toward oxygen and chlorine.
sqs.a:
Na is more reactive than Mg because:

  • Lower IE₁: Na (494 kJ/mol) vs Mg (738 kJ/mol) → Na loses electron more easily.
  • Only 1 valence electron vs Mg's 2 → Na achieves noble gas configuration more readily.
  • Larger atomic radius → valence electron more weakly held.

With O₂: Na burns more vigorously, producing peroxide Na₂O₂; Mg burns to give MgO only.
With Cl₂: Na reacts with yellow flame; Mg reacts but less vigorously (MgCl₂).

sqs.q: Why is IE of Li much lower than He, despite Li having higher nuclear charge (+3 vs +2)?
sqs.a:
Li's valence electron is in the 2nd shell (farther from nucleus) vs He's electrons in the 1st shell (very close).

Shielding in Li: The 1s² core electrons shield the 2s electron from the full +3 charge → Zeff felt by Li's outer electron is only ~+1.3.

He: Both electrons are in the 1st shell experiencing the full +2 charge with no shielding → very stable → very high IE.

sqs.q: IE of Be (Z=4) is higher than B (Z=5) despite lower nuclear charge. Explain.
sqs.a:
Be (1s²2s²): fully-filled 2s subshell — extra stable. Both 2s electrons experience the full nuclear charge with no inter-subshell shielding.

B (1s²2s²2p¹): outermost electron in 2p subshell — higher energy than 2s, and shielded by the 2s² electrons below it → effective nuclear charge on B's outer electron is less than on Be's 2s electrons.

Therefore Be's 2s electron is held more tightly → IE(Be) > IE(B).

sqs.q: What is common in Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Ne, F⁻? Arrange in increasing order of size.
sqs.a:
Common: All are isoelectronic — each has exactly 10 electrons (configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶).

Increasing order of ionic radius:

Al³⁺ < Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < Ne ≈ F⁻

Reason: All have 10 electrons but different proton counts. More protons → stronger pull → smaller size. Al³⁺ (13 protons) is smallest; F⁻ (9 protons) is largest.

sqs.q: Calculate the oxidation number of S in SO₂ and SO₃.
sqs.a:
In SO₂: S + 2(−2) = 0 → S = +4

S uses 4 of its 6 valence electrons for bonding with 2 oxygen atoms.

In SO₃: S + 3(−2) = 0 → S = +6

S uses all 6 valence electrons (possible because S can expand its octet using empty 3d orbitals).

sqs.q: Explain why F has lower electron affinity than Cl despite F being smaller.
sqs.a:
Although F is smaller (so we'd expect a stronger pull on the incoming electron), F has a less negative EA than Cl.

Reason: F's 2p orbitals are extremely compact and crowded. When an extra electron enters the already-crowded 2p subshell, it experiences strong electron-electron repulsion → less energy released.

Cl has larger 3p orbitals → incoming electron experiences less repulsion → more energy released → more negative EA.

Values: Cl = −349 kJ/mol (more negative); F = −328 kJ/mol.

lqs.title: Q3 — Reactions of Na and Mg (Long Q Pattern)
lqs.q: Describe the reactions of Na and Mg with (a) water, (b) oxygen, (c) chlorine. Compare their reactivities.

parts.label: PART (a) — With Water
points: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ (vigorous, exothermic; golden flame)
Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂ (slow with cold water)
Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂ (vigorous with steam only)

parts.label: PART (b) — With Oxygen
points: 2Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O₂ (main product: sodium peroxide; golden flame)
4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (limited O₂ only)
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO (intense white flame; white product)

parts.label: PART (c) — With Chlorine
points: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl (vigorous; yellow flame; white solid NaCl)
Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂ (white solid; less vigorous)

parts.label: COMPARISON OF REACTIVITY — Na > Mg
points: Na has lower IE₁ (494 vs 738 kJ/mol) → loses electron more easily
Na has larger atomic radius → valence electron more weakly held
Na has only 1 valence electron (Mg has 2) → achieves stable config more easily
Na reacts vigorously with cold water; Mg needs steam — confirms greater reactivity of Na

lqs.title: Q4 — Acidic and Basic Nature of Period 3 Oxides/Chlorides
lqs.q: Explain the acidic and basic nature of oxides and chlorides of Period 3 elements with examples.

parts.label: PART (a) — Bonding Trend in Period 3 Oxides
points: Groups 1–3: ionic oxides (Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃) — large EN difference with O
Groups 4–7: covalent oxides (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, SO₃) — small EN difference

parts.label: PART (b) — Classification of Oxides
points: Basic oxides (Groups 1–2): react with water → alkalis: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂
Acidic oxides (Groups 4–7): react with water → acids: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; react with bases
Amphoteric oxide: Al₂O₃ — reacts with both HCl (→ AlCl₃ + H₂O) and NaOH (→ NaAlO₂ + H₂O)

parts.label: PART (c) — Classification of Chlorides
points: Neutral: NaCl (Na⁺ large, low charge → no hydrolysis → pH=7)
Acidic: AlCl₃ (Al³⁺ small, high charge → hydrolyses water → releases H⁺)
Strongly acidic: SiCl₄ + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 4HCl; PCl₃ + 3H₂O → H₃PO₃ + 3HCl

quiz.q: Period number of an element tells us its:
quiz.exp: Period number = shell number (n). E.g., Period 3 → 3 shells → outermost electrons in 3rd shell.

quiz.q: Which property DECREASES across a period (left to right)?
quiz.exp: Atomic radius decreases across a period — nuclear charge increases, same shell number, electrons pulled closer.

quiz.q: Which property INCREASES going down a group?
quiz.exp: Metallic character increases down a group — atomic size and shielding increase → easier to lose electrons.

quiz.q: The first ionization energy of N is HIGHER than O because:
opts: N has a half-filled 2p (extra stable); O has a paired electron causing repulsion
quiz.exp: N (2p³) has half-filled 2p — extra stable. O (2p⁴) has a paired electron that experiences spin-pair repulsion → easier to remove → lower IE than N.

quiz.q: Electron affinity of Cl is MORE negative than F because:
opts: F's compact 2p orbitals cause strong electron repulsion when gaining e⁻
Cl is in a lower period
quiz.exp: F's very compact 2p orbitals are crowded — an incoming electron experiences strong repulsion → less energy released. Cl has larger 3p orbitals → less repulsion → more energy released.

quiz.q: The correct book value of ΔH°ea2 for O²⁻ formation is:
quiz.exp: The book has a printing error (says 798). The correct value is +844 kJ/mol — positive because adding e⁻ to already-negative O⁻ requires energy input.

quiz.q: Isoelectronic species Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ all have 10 electrons. Their size order is:
quiz.exp: All have 10 electrons. More protons = stronger pull = smaller size. Al³⁺ (13p) is smallest; Na⁺ (11p) is largest of the three.

quiz.q: The electronegativity of F is 4.0. The element with the LOWEST electronegativity is:
quiz.exp: Cs has the lowest electronegativity (0.8) — it is the largest stable alkali metal with the most shielding, holding bonding electrons least strongly. (Fr is less stable/radioactive.)

quiz.q: Na burns in excess O₂ to form mainly:
quiz.exp: When Na burns in excess O₂, the main product is sodium peroxide Na₂O₂ (golden-yellow flame). Na₂O only forms under limited O₂ conditions.

quiz.q: Mg reacts with COLD water to give:
quiz.exp: Mg reacts slowly with cold water: Mg + 2H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂. With steam it reacts vigorously to give MgO + H₂.

quiz.q: Al₂O₃ is classified as:
quiz.exp: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric — it reacts with both acids (HCl → AlCl₃) and bases (NaOH → NaAlO₂). Al is in Group 13, on the metal/non-metal boundary.

quiz.q: Which Period 3 chloride gives an acidic solution in water?
quiz.exp: AlCl₃ undergoes hydrolysis: AlCl₃ + 3H₂O → Al(OH)₃ + 3HCl. Al³⁺ (small, high charge) polarises water → releases H⁺ → acidic solution.

quiz.q: Oxidation state of S in SO₄²⁻ is:
P shows oxidation states +3 and +5 because:
opts: P has empty 3d orbitals available for octet expansion
quiz.exp: P has empty 3d orbitals. Electrons can be promoted into them from ground state → can use 3 electrons (PCl₃, +3) or 5 electrons (PCl₅, +5) for bonding.

quiz.q: Which element has the highest first ionization energy in Period 3?
quiz.exp: Ar (noble gas) has a completely filled outer shell (3s²3p⁶) → most stable → highest IE in Period 3.

quiz.q: IE of Be > IE of B because:
opts: Be has fully-filled 2s (extra stable); B's 2p electron is shielded and at higher energy
quiz.exp: Be (1s²2s²) has fully-filled 2s — extra stable. B (1s²2s²2p¹) has its outer electron in 2p, which is shielded by 2s² and at higher energy → easier to remove → lower IE.

quiz.q: Across Period 3, the bonding in oxides changes from:
quiz.exp: Groups 1–3 form ionic oxides (large EN difference with O). Groups 4–7 form covalent oxides (small EN difference with O). Bonding shifts ionic → covalent across the period.

quiz.q: The equation 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl describes a reaction where Na burns with:
quiz.exp: Sodium burns with a characteristic golden-yellow flame. The product NaCl is a white solid. Na imparts a golden-yellow colour to flames due to its emission spectrum.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a factor affecting atomic radius?
quiz.exp: Neutron number has no direct effect on atomic radius (neutrons are in the nucleus and don't interact with electrons). The three factors are: number of shells, Z_eff, and shielding effect.

quiz.q: The second electron affinity of oxygen is ENDOTHERMIC (+844 kJ/mol). The FIRST electron affinity is:
quiz.exp: The 1st EA of O is −142 kJ/mol — exothermic (energy released). Adding the 1st electron to a neutral atom is energetically favourable. The 2nd EA is endothermic because the O⁻ ion repels the incoming electron.
